steps.prompt: What actually runs a VR game?
steps.sub: Before any sword-swinging or spell-casting, every VR game is the same tiny cycle repeated 72 times a second. By the end you'll know the base you build on and be able to trace one frame from controller to headset.

steps.prompt: You open Unity to start a VR game. What's the very first base you need before any gameplay?

options.t: A finished 3D level with enemies already placed
Unity + the Meta XR SDK + an XR rig (a camera + hands that follow the headset)
A multiplayer server so friends can join

steps.why: The base is Unity (the engine), the Meta XR SDK (the bridge to the Quest's tracking), and an XR rig — a camera and hand objects that move with the real headset and controllers. Levels, enemies, and multiplayer all come later and need this base to even render.
hints: You can't place enemies in a world the headset can't see yet. What lets Unity talk to the Quest?
Think 'engine + the SDK that reads the headset + the rig that becomes your eyes and hands'.

steps.prompt: The base of a VR game has 3 layers.
steps.sub: Tap each card. These three stack up before you write a line of gameplay.

cards.b: The game engine — it renders 3D, runs physics, and calls your code every frame.
The bridge to the Quest: head & hand tracking, controller buttons, the VR display.
A camera that is your eyes + two hand objects that follow your real controllers in the scene.

steps.prompt: Sort each piece: is it part of the BASE you set up first, or GAMEPLAY you add later?
steps.sub: Tap an item, then a bin.

items.t: Make a sword you can grab
Set the Unity project to Android / Quest

hints: If the headset couldn't even render without it, it's base.
A sword and zombies are fun stuff — but they need the rig and SDK to exist first.

steps.prompt: Now the heart of it: a VR game is really ONE thing repeated ~72 times a second. What is that one thing called?
steps.sub: This repeated cycle is the engine's heartbeat.

options.t: The game loop — input → update → render, once per frame

steps.why: The game loop is the per-frame cycle: read input, update the world, draw it. Unity runs it for you — your Update() code is one slice of it. Rendering and physics are steps INSIDE the loop, not the loop itself.
hints: It's the whole cycle, not one stage of it.
Input, then update the world, then draw — over and over. What's the name for that cycle?

steps.sub: Tap each. This trio runs every single frame.

cards.b: Read the headset pose and controllers: where are the hands, is the trigger held?
Move the world: physics steps, enemy AI thinks, your grabbed sword follows your hand.
Draw the scene twice — once per eye — and send it to the headset display.

steps.prompt: Tap the 3 jobs in the order they run in a single frame.
steps.sub: Then the whole thing repeats next frame.
chips: Render the scene to both eyes
hints: You can't move the world based on a trigger press you haven't read yet.
Sense first, then change the world, then show the result. Input → update → render.

steps.prompt: Walk one frame through the loop — the player flicks their wrist to swing a sword.
steps.sub: Pick the next move at each step. The frame log fills in as you go.
steps.goal: Render one correct frame at 72fps while the player swings.

turns.situation: A new frame begins. The player has moved their controller and is holding the trigger.
turns.q: What does the loop do FIRST?
options: Read input: new hand position + trigger held

turns.situation: It now knows the hand's new position and that the sword is grabbed.
turns.q: What's next, before anything is drawn?
options: Update: move the sword to follow the hand, run physics
Render immediately with the old sword position
turns.log: ⚙️ Update → sword follows hand, physics steps

turns.situation: The world is now up to date for this instant — sword in its new pose.
turns.q: What's the last job of this frame?
options: Render the scene to both eyes and show it
Wait for the next button press
turns.log: 🖼️ Render → drawn per-eye, sent to headset

turns.situation: The frame is done in under ~13.9 ms (the budget for 72fps).
options: Loop again → start the next frame's input

hints: Same order every frame: input → update → render.
72fps means each full loop must finish in about 13.9 milliseconds.

steps.sub: Tap each, then check all at once.

statements.t: If a frame takes too long, the headset drops below 72fps and players can feel sick.
statements.why: Right — VR is unforgiving. Miss the ~13.9 ms frame budget and the world judders, which causes real motion sickness. Holding 72fps is a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have.

statements.t: You write the game loop yourself with a giant while(true).
statements.why: No — Unity owns the loop. You hook into it by putting code in Update() (and FixedUpdate() for physics). Unity calls those for you every frame.

statements.t: Input always has to be read before you update the world for that frame.
statements.why: Yes — you can't move the sword to follow a hand you haven't read yet. Input feeds update, update feeds render.

hints: Think about why a stutter in VR feels so much worse than on a flat screen.
Who actually calls Update() — you, or the engine?
